provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation:
The scene has one long marker line in colour palette[8]. It is crossed by several full-length coloured lines, and each crossing cell is palette[1]. Reflections keep the marker line on the same axis, and an odd number of rotations swaps the axis. So the factory checks d4 parity: an even value gives a vertical marker column, an odd value gives a horizontal marker row. It then emits a program written directly for that orientation.

The emitted program works like this:
- It finds the marker as the column (or row) with the most palette[8] cells.
- The crossing lines are the perpendicular rows (or columns) whose cell on the marker is palette[1]. A line's colour is the most common value in that line other than palette[1].
- Every row (or column) is filled with the colour of its nearest crossing line. An exact distance tie between two different colours gives a full line of palette[1]. A tie between lines of the same colour keeps that colour.
- The marker becomes palette[1].
- Each crossing line becomes palette[1] everywhere, except the cell on the marker, which becomes palette[8].

This reproduces the generator's banding: its offset of 2 for different colours leaves the integer midpoint as 1, and its offset of 0 for equal colours fills the midpoint. Distance is symmetric, so reflections need no direction change. Colour roles are palette constants, and line colours are read from the pixels.
draft_notes.limitations: No tests were run. If there are no crossing lines, the output is all palette[1] apart from the marker. That case is outside the generator's domain, which always has 2 to 4 lines. The program assumes, as the generator guarantees, that the marker line is the unique longest run of palette[8] and that palette[1] never appears as a line colour. No fixture contradicts the uniform rule.
